# The Compute Frontier: Bandwidth, Not FLOPs {#sec-compute-frontier}

@sec-accelerators-networking introduced arithmetic intensity, the number of
operations a kernel performs per byte it moves, and the bandwidth tiers inside
an accelerator cluster. This chapter turns those ideas into a method for
locating a system's limit. Its working thesis is that the frontier's scarce
resource is bytes rather than arithmetic. The thesis is not universal. It can
be checked only against a named workload, a named memory boundary, and the
measured traffic that crosses that boundary. A matrix multiplication with
enough reuse can exhaust the arithmetic units; token-by-token inference can
instead wait on weights, on the KV cache that stores attention keys and values
for earlier tokens, or on a collective. “Bandwidth-bound” is therefore a
diagnosis made for one workload on one system.

The diagnosis depends on where the boundaries sit, and two recent changes have
moved them: accelerators have become chiplet packages, and the NVLink boundary
has moved from a chassis to a multi-node domain in one prominent system.
NVLink is NVIDIA's direct GPU-to-GPU link. Each change moves a boundary and
changes the cost of crossing it. Data still crosses the moved
boundary, which becomes a new place to measure.

## The frontier is a vector of bounds

The original Roofline model compares a kernel's operational intensity with
peak compute and memory bandwidth [@williams2009roofline]. A frontier system
needs more than one roofline because bytes can cross several boundaries. One
optimistic lower bound for a step is

$$
T_{\text{step}}
\ge
\max\left(
  \frac{F}{P_{\text{eff}}},
  \frac{Q_{\text{HBM}}}{B_{\text{HBM}}},
  \frac{Q_{\text{up}}}{B_{\text{up}}},
  \frac{Q_{\text{out}}}{B_{\text{out}}}
\right).
$$

where:

- $F$ is the useful arithmetic work and $P_{\text{eff}}$ is the effective,
  workload-specific arithmetic rate;
- $Q_{\text{HBM}}$ is traffic volume between the processor and HBM, the
  stacked high-bandwidth memory packaged beside it, while $B_{\text{HBM}}$ is
  sustainable bandwidth at that boundary;
- $Q_{\text{up}}$ and $B_{\text{up}}$ describe traffic and sustainable
  bandwidth inside the scale-up domain, the group of accelerators joined by
  the fastest device fabric; and
- $Q_{\text{out}}$ and $B_{\text{out}}$ describe traffic and sustainable
  bandwidth across the scale-out fabric, the network that connects those
  groups.

The largest term, called the binding term below, identifies the first
optimization target. The equation is a lower bound rather than a latency
prediction, because it assumes perfect overlap among independent transfers and
computation. Dependencies, queuing, synchronization, protocol overhead, and
contention can make observed time larger; phases that cannot overlap may need
to be added rather than maximized. A datasheet peak does not substitute for
$P_{\text{eff}}$ or for any sustainable bandwidth.

:::: {.runnable}
```python
# Illustrative units: work in operations, traffic in bytes, rates per second.
terms = {
    "arithmetic": 2.0e15 / 1.0e15,
    "HBM traffic": 8.0e12 / 3.0e12,
    "scale-up traffic": 1.0e12 / 9.0e11,
    "scale-out traffic": 5.0e11 / 2.0e11,
}

for name, seconds in terms.items():
    print(f"{name:18s} {seconds:.2f} s")

binding = max(terms, key=terms.get)
print(f"Binding term: {binding}")
```
::::

```{figure}
//| figure: roofline
//| label: fig-compute-frontier-bounds
//| fig-cap: "The first two terms of the bound for one kernel at the HBM boundary, drawn as a roofline on log-log axes. Attainable throughput is min(P, I·B), so a kernel whose arithmetic intensity I lies left of the ridge I* = P / B is bound by bytes and one to its right by arithmetic; the bars read the same bound as time. The ceilings are dense BF16 datasheet peaks, not the sustainable rates the bound calls for. Example operations use BF16 operands and count each operand crossing HBM once, the best case for their shapes."
```

This model also explains why lowering precision is not automatically a speedup.
It helps when it reduces the binding traffic or increases the binding compute
rate. Extra conversion, padding, metadata, or an unchanged KV-cache path can
leave the largest term where it was.

## The package moves the memory boundary

A reticle field limits the area that lithography exposes in one image. A large
monolithic die near that limit is expensive to grow and vulnerable to defects.
Splitting logic into chiplets can improve yield and reuse, but it adds
die-to-die links, packaging work, and new failure surfaces. The interposer
provides dense wiring among compute dies and HBM stacks; the package substrate
connects that assembly to power and board-level signals. The interposer and
the substrate are two distinct physical layers.

This is the @gls-cowos package: an advanced package that places compute
chiplets and HBM on one silicon interposer. TSMC documents CoWoS as a family of
integration technologies and describes interposers larger than a single
reticle field [@tsmc2026cowos]. The documentation supports a claim about
packaging direction; it gives no basis for extrapolating a vendor roadmap into
exact future system capacity.

```{dot}
//| label: fig-compute-frontier-package
//| fig-cap: "The memory boundary is built from several physical layers. An interposer links compute chiplets and HBM stacks; a package substrate carries the assembly to the board."
digraph package {
  rankdir=TB;
  bgcolor="transparent";
  graph [nodesep=0.35, ranksep=0.45];
  node [shape=box, style="rounded,filled", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=10,
        color="#6b7280", fontcolor="#6b7280", fillcolor="#f1ece1", penwidth=1.1];
  edge [color="#6b7280", arrowsize=0.7];

  subgraph cluster_top {
    label="on the interposer";
    color="#9ca3af";
    compute [label="compute\nchiplets"];
    hbm [label="HBM\nstacks"];
  }
  interposer [label="silicon interposer\ndense die-to-die wiring",
              color="#3b82f6", fontcolor="#3b82f6", penwidth=1.4];
  substrate [label="package substrate\npower + board signals"];
  board [label="accelerator board"];

  compute -> interposer;
  hbm -> interposer;
  interposer -> substrate -> board;
}
```

HBM adds several separate quantities to the design:

- **Memory capacity** determines how much parameter, activation, optimizer, and
  KV-cache state can reside near the processors.
- **Sustainable bandwidth** is the rate a real access pattern reaches, after
  accounting for controllers, locality, concurrency, and protocol effects.
- **Traffic volume** is created by the algorithm, tensor layout, precision,
  recomputation policy, and cache behavior.
- **Energy per bit** makes unnecessary movement a power and cooling cost even
  when latency is hidden.

HBM4 documentation gives a product-scoped example. SK hynix and Micron
describe a 2,048-bit interface, twice the previous generation's width
[@skhynix2025hbm4; @micron2026hbm4]. HBM4 also introduces a more capable base
die beneath the stacked memory dies. Delivered bandwidth, capacity, yield,
power, and application throughput depend on the complete package and workload,
which the interface width alone does not determine.

That width is one reason HBM sits on a silicon interposer: 2,048 signals per
stack need contacts packed more densely than an ordinary package substrate can
route. The bandwidth of a memory link is the number of signals times the rate
on each, so the same bandwidth can also come from fewer signals that each run
faster. JEDEC's SPHBM4 standard, JESD330-4, published in July 2026, takes that
route. It keeps the HBM4 DRAM dies, and with them the capacity per stack, and
places a new base die beneath them with 512 data signals in place of HBM4's
2,048. The base die uses 4:1 serialization, sending the bits of four signals
in turn over one wire, to reach the same bandwidth [@jedec2026sphbm4].

Fewer signals allow the wider bump pitch, the spacing between the contacts
that join a die to the layer beneath it, that a standard organic package
substrate requires. The stack can then mount on the substrate itself, and the
standard supports a longer channel between processor and memory, which can
leave room for more stacks around the processor. The cost moves from
interposer area to signaling: each remaining signal runs at four times the
rate, the base die and the processor's memory interface must drive and receive
it, and energy per bit and signal integrity at that rate become quantities to
measure. In the terms of the evidence labels later in this chapter, SPHBM4 is
an open specification. Which accelerators adopt it, and at what delivered
bandwidth and power, only product evidence can show.

In the terms of the four HBM quantities above, the memory wall is the case in
which effective arithmetic rate grows faster than sustainable HBM bandwidth, so
the arithmetic intensity required to become compute-bound rises. That rising arithmetic-intensity floor
affects only work below it; kernels with sufficient reuse can remain
compute-bound.

## The scale-up boundary can span multiple nodes

A **scale-up domain** is the set of accelerators connected by the system's
lowest-latency, highest-bandwidth device fabric. A **scale-out fabric**
connects those domains. Whether traffic stays inside a domain or crosses the
scale-out fabric changes collective latency, bisection bandwidth, routing,
congestion, and the cost of a failure. The two terms name roles, and different
systems implement each role with different topologies.

NVIDIA's DGX GB200 NVL72 is a current, product-scoped example. Its official
documentation describes a 72-GPU NVLink domain in one rack, with 18 compute
trays, nine NVLink switch trays, and a passive copper cable backplane
[@nvidia2026dgxgb200]. The accompanying tuning guide describes the system as an
expansion beyond earlier eight-GPU scale-up systems
[@nvidia2026multinode]. The protocol boundary is the NVLink domain rather
than the cabinet, since other reference layouts can distribute that domain
differently. The dense wiring does not make 72 GPUs one device; software still
manages separate memory, processes, address spaces, logical topology,
synchronization, and a multi-node failure domain.

```{dot}
//| label: fig-compute-frontier-domain
//| fig-cap: "A multi-node scale-up fabric enlarges the fast locality domain, but software still maps process groups and collectives onto physical links. Crossing the scale-out edge changes both performance and failure behavior."
digraph domain {
  rankdir=TB;
  bgcolor="transparent";
  node [shape=box, style="rounded,filled", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=9,
        color="#6b7280", fontcolor="#6b7280", fillcolor="#f1ece1", penwidth=1.1];
  edge [fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=9, color="#6b7280", fontcolor="#6b7280"];

  graph [compound=true, pad=0.06];
  subgraph cluster_up {
    label="scale-up\ndomain";
    color="#3b82f6";
    gpu1 [label="GPU-local\nmemory + work"];
    sw [label="scale-up\nswitch fabric"];
    gpu2 [label="peer GPU\nmemory + work"];
    gpu1 -> sw [dir=both, label="fast collective"];
    sw -> gpu2 [dir=both];
  }
  out [label="scale-out fabric\nInfiniBand / Ethernet"];
  peer [label="another domain"];
  sw -> out [label="domain edge"];
  out -> peer;
}
```

Each form of parallelism produces its own traffic. Tensor parallel groups
often run frequent all-reduces; expert parallel groups exchange routed token
data; pipeline parallel stages send activations; data parallel replicas
synchronize gradients or parameters. Message size, frequency, overlap,
collective algorithm, model shape, and contention determine which group
benefits most from the fast domain, so placement should follow measured
traffic rather than a fixed rule per parallelism type. The sound procedure is
to measure each edge, map the heaviest latency-sensitive communication onto
the logical topology, and then verify end-to-end time.

UALink is a family of open scale-up specifications. Its 200G 1.0
specification defines a 200 Gb/s-per-lane interface and a switched domain of
up to 1,024 accelerators [@ualink2025spec]. A second set, published in April
2026, consists of a Common 2.0 specification that adds in-network compute
(operations performed inside the switch fabric), 200G data-link and
physical-layer 2.0 specifications split out from the common specification, and
first manageability and chiplet specifications [@ualink2026spec20]. The
versioned documents give builders a common target. A published specification
does not establish that every switch, cable, software stack, or large
deployment it describes is available, and a multi-vendor fabric also needs
tests showing that separate implementations interoperate.

At rack-to-rack distance, scale-out networks already use optics. Co-packaged
optics changes where electrical-to-optical conversion happens: placing optical
engines near switch silicon shortens the lossy electrical channel and can
reduce faceplate-density pressure. It also couples optics to a hot, expensive
package. Reliability, laser placement, test, repair, and serviceability then
become architectural questions [@minkenberg2021cpo]. Moving the conversion
point leaves the extent of the NVLink domain unchanged.

Optical circuit switching reconfigures the physical paths themselves. TPU v4
is a documented deployed example of optical circuit switches changing a large
system's topology [@jouppi2023tpuv4]. A proposal such as Opus instead
reconfigures optical rails at parallelism-phase boundaries and remains a
research prototype [@ding2026opus]. Under either technology, communication
remains a term in the lower bound.

## Architecture choices move a term of the bound

Accelerator designs can be compared by which term in the lower bound above
they change and which cost they expose elsewhere.

A conventional HBM accelerator keeps a large software surface and targets many
tensor shapes. Its package offers high external-memory capacity and bandwidth,
but weights and activations still cross the HBM boundary. A custom accelerator
can co-design dataflow, compiler, memory, and network for a narrower workload;
the gain depends on whether that workload resembles the design target.

Wafer-scale integration puts the locality boundary in a different place.
Cerebras' architecture distributes SRAM and compute across a wafer-scale
device and uses dedicated on- and off-wafer interconnects [@lie2023cerebras].
That can
increase locality and on-device bandwidth, but SRAM capacity, defect
management, compilation, system I/O, and multi-system scaling remain
constraints. “No HBM” removes one named boundary; the state and its movement
remain.

Technology claims should therefore carry an evidence status. As of 23
September 2026, this chapter uses these labels:

| Status | What the label establishes | What it does not establish |
|---|---|---|
| **Available system** | Shipping documentation, accessible service, or independent deployment evidence identifies a usable system. | That every configuration is generally available or achieves peak claims. |
| **Announced product** | A vendor has named a product and intended capabilities or schedule. | Shipment, sustained performance, reliability, or schedule. |
| **Research prototype** | A paper or demonstration establishes an implemented idea under stated conditions. | Production readiness, fleet operability, or economic viability. |
| **Open specification** | A versioned interface contract is published. | Interoperable products, software maturity, or deployment scale. |

For example, the NVL72 rack above is an available system documented by its
operator guide. Opus is a research prototype [@ding2026opus]. The UALink
specifications, 1.0 and the 2.0 set, are open specifications. A vendor roadmap
counts only as an announced product until dated production or deployment
evidence supports a different label. These labels can change; the cited
evidence should change with them.

::: {.callout-note .dated}
## As of September 2026

Vendors state scale-up domains of the following sizes. Each counts the domain
at its own boundary and over its own topology, so equal counts do not imply
equal bandwidth or equal failure behavior.

- NVIDIA GB200 and GB300 NVL72: 72 GPUs in one NVLink domain per rack, in a
  rack guide updated on 17 September 2026 [@nvidia2026dgxgb200]. Available
  system.
- NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72: 72 Rubin GPUs and 36 Vera CPUs joined by
  sixth-generation NVLink [@nvidia2026verarubin]. Status discussed below.
- AMD Helios: 72 Instinct MI455X GPUs per rack, which AMD described on 23 July
  2026 as "now in production", with OpenAI expecting to bring Helios online
  from the fourth quarter of 2026 [@amd2026aai]. Announced product with a
  vendor production claim.
- Google TPU7x (Ironwood): a 9,216-chip pod, documented as the latest TPU
  available on Google Cloud [@google2026tpu7x]. Available system. Google
  announced TPU 8t, with up to 9,600 chips per superpod, and TPU 8i, with 1,152
  chips per pod, on 22 April 2026 without an availability date
  [@google2026tpu8]. Announced products.
- AWS Trn3 UltraServer: up to 144 Trainium3 chips, announced as generally
  available on 2 December 2025 [@aws2025trn3]. Available system.

Vera Rubin shows how the labels apply while a product ramps. On 26 August
2026 NVIDIA stated that the platform "is ramping into full production with
racks running at partners including CoreWeave, Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure,
Oracle Cloud Infrastructure and Nebius" [@nvidia2026q2fy27]. Its first MLPerf
Inference result, in round v6.1 on 16 September 2026, was a preview submission
[@nvidia2026rubinmlperf]. Under the benchmark's rules, a preview system has not
yet qualified as available, and its submitter commits to publishing results for
it as an available system by the first submission round at least 140 days
later [@mlcommons2026rules]. Both statements come from NVIDIA. An operator guide, a
generally available service, or independent deployment evidence would move the
rack to the available-system label.

The UALink consortium's April 2026 release names no shipping silicon and says
the consortium "plans to introduce interoperability and compliance programs"
[@ualink2026spec20].
:::

## Prefill and decode are workload phases

Prefill processes a prompt in parallel across its sequence length. Decode
usually advances one or a few positions at a time while reading model state
and the KV cache. This often gives prefill more reuse and decode lower
arithmetic intensity, but the result is conditional. Batch size, sequence
length, model architecture, quantization, tensor shape, kernel fusion, cache
layout, and parallel placement can move either phase between bounds.

Splitting the phases across different device pools can specialize capacity,
bandwidth, and scheduling. Some accelerators are built for one phase: NVIDIA
describes Rubin GPUs as handling large-scale context processing, its term for
prefill, while its LPX accelerators handle latency-sensitive decode
[@nvidia2026lpx], and Huawei designed its Ascend 950PR for prefill and
recommendation and its 950DT for decode and training [@huawei2025atlas950].
The split also creates a phase boundary: KV-cache state
must be transferred or made remotely accessible, requests must be routed, and
the two pools must be balanced under a changing workload. A design is better
only if saved compute or memory time exceeds transfer, queueing, and
under-utilization costs. @sec-memory-scheduling develops those serving
tradeoffs; @sec-machine-breaks follows their operational failure modes.

## Escape routes change a named term

The mechanisms for escaping a bandwidth limit can be combined, and each
trades one resource for another.

| Lever | Term it tries to change | Typical cost or new check |
|---|---|---|
| **Reduce traffic** with lower precision, fusion, compression, or reuse | Lower $Q_{\text{HBM}}$, $Q_{\text{up}}$, or $Q_{\text{out}}$ | Numerical quality, metadata, conversion overhead, and kernel support |
| **Increase locality** with larger caches, SRAM, tiling, or fusion | Keep repeated bytes inside a cheaper boundary | Capacity, compilation constraints, and lost flexibility |
| **Increase sustainable bandwidth** with wider memory or a faster fabric | Raise one measured $B$ | Package area, power, signaling reach, yield, and cost |
| **Distribute state** through sharding or phase specialization | Reduce per-device capacity and traffic pressure | More communication, coordination, imbalance, and failure behavior |
| **Change the physical link** with optics or a reconfigurable topology | Raise reach or reduce network energy per bit | Serviceability, reconfiguration delay, reliability, and control complexity |

```{dot}
//| label: fig-compute-frontier-escape-map
//| fig-cap: "An escape route is useful only when it changes the binding term. Every route creates a cost that must be measured at the same workload boundary."
digraph escape_map {
  rankdir=TB;
  bgcolor="transparent";
  node [shape=box, style="rounded,filled", fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=10,
        color="#6b7280", fontcolor="#6b7280", fillcolor="#f1ece1", penwidth=1.1];
  edge [fontname="Helvetica", fontsize=9, color="#6b7280", fontcolor="#6b7280"];

  bound [label="measured\nbinding term", color="#3b82f6", fontcolor="#3b82f6", penwidth=1.4];
  levers [label="change one named term\n\nreduce traffic\nincrease locality\nincrease sustainable bandwidth\ndistribute state"];
  verify [label="remeasure step time,\nquality, power, cost"];

  bound -> levers -> verify;
}
```

@sec-quantization-kernels explains when FP8 and FP4 reduce bytes without
unacceptable numerical loss. @sec-powering-ai follows the energy and cooling
cost when the chosen escape route adds packages, links, or conversion.

## How to compare frontier systems

A hardware comparison should state the conditions under which each number
was measured, rather than set two peak numbers side by side. Record at least:

1. the model and operation being measured;
2. tensor shape, batch size, and sequence length;
3. precision for inputs, weights, accumulation, communication, and stored
   state;
4. software version, compiler flags, kernels, and communication libraries;
5. device count, placement, physical and logical topology, and competing
   traffic;
6. traffic volume and sustained bandwidth at each relevant boundary;
7. latency and throughput distributions after warm-up, not only a best run;
8. the power boundary: chip, board, rack, cooling overhead, or facility;
9. availability, failure behavior, repair assumptions, and recovery time; and
10. cost scope, currency, utilization, and time horizon.

Measure in three passes. First, microbenchmark each boundary with the same
message sizes and access patterns the workload uses. Second, profile the
important kernels and collectives to estimate the terms in
the lower bound above. Third, run the end-to-end workload and explain
the gap between the lower bound and observed time. A claimed improvement is
credible when the named binding term falls, the end-to-end result follows,
and quality and reliability remain inside the stated acceptance limits.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Constraint arrow

When effective compute grows faster than memory and fabric bandwidth, the
rising arithmetic-intensity floor pushes pressure upward. Packaging determines
how much memory can sit near compute; topology determines which parallel groups
share the fast domain; serving determines whether state is reused or moved.
Those links hand off to @sec-making-silicon, @sec-memory-scheduling, and
@sec-powering-ai. Each link can be tested by naming the boundary, measuring
its traffic, changing one term, and measuring again.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## What's contested

- **How large should the scale-up domain be?** A larger domain can keep more
  collectives on a fast fabric, but it increases switch, cable, power, cooling,
  and failure-domain costs. Which size pays off depends on the workload's
  traffic pattern, which GPU count alone does not describe.
- **Must scale-up use a proprietary fabric?** Proprietary systems are deployed;
  UALink publishes an open contract; Ethernet-derived designs reuse a broad
  component ecosystem. Comparing them requires implementations measured at
  the same message sizes, topology, software maturity, and availability.
- **When should optics enter the package?** Co-packaging can improve electrical
  reach and energy, while pluggable optics preserves replacement boundaries.
  Fleet reliability and serviceability evidence remains as important as link
  rate.
- **Will specialized or wafer-scale designs displace general accelerators?**
  Specialization can increase locality for a target workload. General systems
  retain value when models, shapes, numerics, or software change. The answer is
  workload- and deployment-specific.
:::

The compute frontier is therefore a set of boundaries whose traffic changes
with the program, and one FLOPs figure set against one bandwidth figure does
not locate the limit. Locating it means finding the active boundary,
distinguishing sustainable rates from peaks, and following the cost of moving
that boundary into the next layer.
